title: The Launch High: Why a Record Sales Week Doesn't Always Mean a More Profitable Coaching Business
linkedin:
A record launch week feels like proof the business is working. The dashboard shows the biggest sales day yet, and it is tempting to read that number as the story.

Here is what we see once the dust settles on a course or coaching launch: the headline number and the actual margin rarely match, because three separate costs settle on three separate clocks.

Ad spend goes out steadily in the weeks before cart open, funding webinars, retargeting and affiliate promotion. Sales land in one concentrated window once the cart opens, which means launch week revenue is being compared to the wrong week's cost from the start.

Then the refund window opens. High-ticket programs commonly carry a fourteen to thirty day money-back guarantee, so a slice of that headline number reverses weeks later, often after it has already been earmarked to fund the next campaign.

Finally, affiliate and joint venture commissions get calculated once refunds settle and paid out in a single batch. Which means the true net result of a launch cannot actually be known on the day the cart closes. It only becomes clear weeks later, by which point the next launch is often already under way.

None of this is an argument against launching. It is an argument for tracking the settled margin per program rather than reacting to day one's number.

If your business runs on course or coaching launches, spring is one of the busiest windows of the year, and a lot of East Coast operators have just come off a strong one. Before treating that headline number as the final word, it is worth knowing where the gaps usually sit.

Ad spend for a launch is mostly paid out in the weeks beforehand, while the sales it generates land in one concentrated week, so comparing launch week revenue to launch week cost alone tends to overstate the result. High-ticket programs commonly carry a money-back guarantee of two to four weeks, so a portion of that revenue is not truly settled until the guarantee period closes. Affiliate or joint venture commissions, where they apply, are usually calculated after that and paid out later again.

Put together, the real return on a launch is rarely knowable on the day the cart closes. The useful habit is tracking the settled margin per program once ad spend, refunds and any partner payouts have cleared, rather than reacting to the first number on the screen.
